vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: work that has piled up and is still waiting to be done
a project started on purpose in order to change something
from the first day of the year until today
to finish work that is late, so that you are on time again
the number of people a team or a company employs
to put a new process in place across a whole team or company
to become the person responsible for something somebody else did
to make a process simpler and faster, with fewer steps

paras: Twelve months ago the finance team in Bogotá had a problem it had learned to live with. Every month the same three reports arrived late, and every month somebody apologised for them in the same meeting, to the same people. Then in January the team took over two more countries. The headcount stayed exactly the same, and the backlog grew from four days to eleven.

In March they started an initiative with a name nobody liked and a goal everybody understood: no report later than day five. They did not buy anything, and they did not ask for one extra person. They rolled out a single template for the three reports, and they cut the number of approvals from four to two. That was the whole plan. By June they had caught up. Year to date, not one of the three reports has been late.

What has changed since then is harder to see on a chart. The team has streamlined eleven other steps, most of them small, and nobody had to be convinced to do it — because once the first change worked, the argument was already over. Two people have been promoted. Nobody has left. The meeting where somebody used to apologise every month does not exist any more.

Ask the manager what she learned and she gives an answer that sounds too simple to be worth writing down. “We did not fix eleven things,” she says. “We fixed one thing, in March, and we have fixed the rest since then. The difference is that in March I had to explain why to everybody in the room. Now nobody asks me why. They ask me which one is next.”

listenings.text: Before the year-end review, one piece of advice, and it is the only one that matters. When somebody asks you how the year went, do not give them a list of months. I have sat through forty of these reviews and the list of months is always the same shape: in January we did this, in February we did that, and by minute four everybody has stopped listening. Give them two sentences instead. The first one is what changed, and it is in the past: we rolled out the new template in March. The second one is what is still true today, and it is not in the past: since then, not one report has been late. That is the whole structure. What happened, and what is still happening because of it. If you can only remember one thing from this recording, remember that the second sentence is the one they will repeat to their own boss.

I was asked last week how long it took us to fix the reporting, and I gave the wrong answer. I said three months, because that is what the calendar says. March to June. But that is not really the answer, and I have thought about it since. It took three months to catch up on the backlog. It has taken a year for the team to stop asking permission before improving something, and honestly that part is not finished. Two people have been promoted, nobody has left, and eleven small steps have disappeared from the process without a single meeting about any of them. If somebody asks me the same question next year, I am going to say the same thing I should have said last week. The catching up took three months. The change is still going on.
